## Active

### D-149 — The leg id is a library concept, not something hop() invents

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The owner ruling, made before implementation: leg ids should be native to semantic-log, not bound
only to the `hop()` function, since that is just a demo. The library therefore owns the binder, the
id's charset, the propagation convention and the requirement behind it, and `hop()` is one consumer
of the identity rather than its author. The same reasoning moved `readIdentity()` onto the public
surface: the propagation contract is enforced on the way out by `identityHeaders()` and on the way
in by the rule that a comma-joined duplicate header is not an identity, and leaving the inbound half
to each application meant one subtle rule re-implemented per application. Verified with 2303 of 2303
tap tests at 100% coverage, up from 2258, and a clean lint.

### D-150 — A leg is a scope bound around a call, not a hop parameter

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The plan had `hop()` taking a required `{leg}` option; it is implemented as `bindLeg(id, fn)`
wrapping the call, because the caller's own request-describing records are emitted immediately
before the hop and, with the id bound only inside `hop()`, those records would carry no leg — the
cross-reference the feature exists for would be missing exactly where a reader looks first. `hop()`
still throws when no leg is bound, so an id cannot be forgotten silently: what changed is where the
id is declared, not whether one is required. The ambient context keeps the leg beside the flow and
the logger joins the two when it assembles a record (`flowWithLeg`), because replacing the flow
object at bind time would have detached `step`'s position from the enclosing scope, an object
deliberately shared by reference with every nested scope. Reconsider if a call site needs a leg on
the wire but not on its own records.

### D-151 — The leg id charset is the one that survives all four consumers

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The enforced charset is lowercase letters and digits plus `.`, `-` and `_`, chosen because one
charset has to survive four consumers at once: an HTTP header value, a source grep for the
id-to-file cross-reference, a diagram label needing no escaping, and the `;` that silently breaks a
generated sequence diagram.

### D-152 — A hop is observed at both ends, and the rule is documented

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

This was taken autonomously, with the owner away and instructing to proceed and make good decisions.
A hop is two observations of one leg id, because a leg id names a call site and encodes no endpoint:
the caller's record, emitted inside the leg scope, and the callee's receipt, emitted under the
inbound leg. The owner was offered (A) instrument both ends and document the rule, (B) propagate the
caller's service name as a fourth identity, or (C) infer the caller from leg order, and (A) was
taken. The fixture now logs the request inside each leg and a receipt under the inbound leg, which
added nine protocol records: three receipts, from the hub `/parties`, hubA `/parties` and the proxy,
and six requests, covering hub to fxp quotes, hub to payee quotes and transfers, hubA to fxpA
quotes, and hubA to proxy quotes and transfers. The rationale is that the topology stays a fact at
both ends, the identity model stays as ruled with three headers and neutral ids, and a hop nobody
logged loses its edge visibly instead of inventing one. Reconsider if the lighter contract is wanted
for real applications: (B) costs one more header and needs only one observation, while (C) costs
nothing but makes the topology an inference that is wrong when hops interleave.

### D-153 — The observed-call union is written with the batch, not debounced

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The original ruling said the per-kind union of observed calls is written on a debounce with a flush
on close, with the window as a named option. It was implemented and then removed, because the window
buys nothing: the unions live in the same snapshot file as the template registry, and the durability
requirement says the registry must be on disk before a batch is acknowledged, so the file is already
written once per accepted batch and the union is in it. Debouncing the union half would mean either
writing the file twice per batch, or writing the registry without its unions and then again with
them. What a debounce would add is a window in which observations are not on disk, for a service
whose whole point is that its shape survives a restart. `ServiceOptions.persistDebounceMs` is gone
and the `onClose` flush went with it, since there is never a pending write. Reconsider if the
snapshot ever grows big enough that a per-batch write is a real cost: the answer then is a separate
append-only surface for observations, not a timer.

### D-154 — Diagram lookup is one route, resolved by the reference's shape

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The plan named two routes, `GET /flows/:kind/diagram` and `GET /flows/:id/diagram`, but Fastify
cannot register one pattern twice, so they are one route, `GET /flows/:reference/diagram`, and the
reference's shape decides which store is asked: a ULID is an execution, since nothing else parses as
one, and anything else is a kind. The two 404s stay distinct and legible: `unknown flow kind` lists
the kinds there are, and `flow execution not retained` reports how many are held and how many were
evicted.

### D-155 — A closed execution records its status but never refuses observations

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

This supersedes my own earlier rule that a spent execution takes no further calls. The generated
artifact `docs/observed-flows.md` proved it wrong on the first real run: the payer's sink flushes
before the hub's, so the payer's terminal `transfer complete` reached the service first and the
hub's last four records were refused, losing the hub's own declaration of `hub.transfer.deliver` —
an entire edge of the observed flow — plus three receipts. Arrival order between processes is not
emission order. The terminal status is now recorded as `closed`, a fact about what the emitter
reported, and never refuses an observation; redeliveries are still deduplicated by event id and
retention is still bounded by the cap.

### D-226 — Capabilities, the gate and the call channel now live in semantic-log

> _2026-09-19 · core/semantic-log · active_

Owner decisions after reviewing how much of the call-recording feature had landed in blong-gogo
(callTrace 247 lines, grant 277, callTraceNode 17): (1) the per-execution gate moves into
semantic-log's existing ambient context as AmbientContext.capabilities with
withCapability/enterCapability/capabilityState - a second AsyncLocalStorage and the attach module it
needed are gone, and blong reaches the gate through the vocabulary it already attaches (loadServer),
so a page simply has no capability; (2) the grammar exports a new subpath
@feasibleone/semantic-log/capability holding the gate, the marker codec and the call channel,
keeping ./emitter's surface as it was; (3) the decided capability travels as the cap field of the
existing identity header (x-semantic-trace) rather than a header of its own - one header, one
parser, and the field is dot-separated because the header's own separator is a comma; the gateway
strips an inbound cap before adopting the identity, so a client cannot set one; (4) the grant stays
in blong-gogo - it is bound to the gateway's key material and the dev key, and semantic-log gets no
jose dependency; (5) the call channel and its four phase names move down (semantic-log owns legs and
calls), with the record envelope ( mtid/method) staying in blong; (6) the two headers keep their
blong names (x-blong-grant, and no x-blong-cap at all any more). Net: ~330 lines left blong-gogo,
callTrace.ts is now config + envelope + one seam for the grant, and BrowserLog has no channel at all
(a page has no scope and no store).

### D-229 — The cluster opener is injected into the base, never imported by it

> _2026-09-19 · core/semantic-log · active_

logBase.ts is on the emitter entry, and test/emitter-entry.test.ts walks relative '.ts' specifiers
out of emitter.ts - it matches 'from './x.ts'' and 'import('./x.ts')', so even an erased 'import
type' or a dynamic 'await import' of the service counts, and the service imports fastify. The base
therefore declares ClusterOptions, ClusterOpener, OpenedCluster and ClusterSink itself and takes
'openCluster' as an option that resolves the opener lazily; src/service/cluster.ts implements it. A
log with no cluster configured never loads the service module at all, which is the second reason the
option is a function.

### D-230 — The attachable facade is one object, not a set of wrappers

> _2026-09-19 · core/semantic-log · active_

The root entry (index.ts) is the union of the emitter and service entries, so degrading wrappers
exported by name - readIdentities, withCapability, capabilityState, enterFlow and the rest - would
collide with the emitter's own exports of those names. '@feasibleone/semantic-log/attachable'
exports 'vocabulary' instead: one object whose members pass through to the emitter once attached and
answer 'no identity' until then. test/parity.test.ts asserts the entry imports nothing, which is
what keeps a browser able to load it.

### D-241 — An execution retains one observation per call, not per record

> _2026-09-21 · core/semantic-log · active_

The per-execution cap (DEFAULT_STEP_LIMIT) now bounds calls: observe() keeps the first declaration
and the first receipt of each leg and skips the rest, while still feeding the aggregate on every
record so the counts and timestamps stay as they were. The cap is what protects the instance view
from a flow's volume, and a call site used 29 times in a loop is one call a diagram draws - counting
its records let a single step displace every other step of the flow. truncations() therefore reports
calls dropped, not records.

### D-249 — A leg is the method; the caller is an identity beside it

> _2026-09-22 · core/semantic-log · active_

Ruled by the owner on 2026-09-22, reading a diagram of the gateway realm: the leg id is what a
diagram labels an arrow with, and a label that began with the caller repeated what the arrow ends
already said (`public.gateway.bundle.find` between `public` and `gateway`) while making every label
longer than the arrow it sat on. The leg is therefore the method the call reaches its callee with
(the forwarded wire name, slash and all: `db/gateway.bundle.find`), and the unit that made the call
travels beside it in its own field of the identity - `from`, with `to` naming the receiver it aimed
at and `seq` its position - so nothing is derived from the id: callerOfLeg is gone, an observation
whose identity carries no caller contributes no edge, and a call is paired with its answer by
(method, caller), because two units may call the same method in one execution. The leg grammar
gained a slash for the same reason: it is a method, not a participant name. Rejected: keeping the
caller in the id and hiding it in the diagram, and reading the caller off the id as a fallback - the
derivation D-210 removed, and the writer is never consulted.

### D-251 — A branch is a separate progress chain, not a field on Decision

> _2026-09-23 · core/semantic-log · active_

The plan gave Decision a seq meaning where the branch applied. The implementation instead leaves
Decision exactly as R11 defined it and carries the branch on record.progress.regions, a chain of
RegionMark outermost first. Two reasons. A one-shot rationale that merely reports a branch is not
the same fact as being inside it, so R11's shape, identity and redaction behaviour needed no change
at all. And a record can only report the branch it is innermost in, so the enclosing branch's
alternatives are unknowable unless the whole chain travels with it. Cost: a nested decision carries
two marks, and a diagram nests one alt block inside another.

### D-253 — Names travel, values stay local

> _2026-09-23 · core/semantic-log · active_

A progress point's `data` and a `decide` branch's `values` never leave the process: the identity
(`[POINTS: a,b]`, `[REGION: d=c]`), the wire projection and the ledger all carry names only (R12).
The reason is the identity contract rather than size — a fingerprint that moved when a payload
changed would make two occurrences of one code path look like two templates — and, second, a diagram
is read by people who may not be entitled to the values. The consequence for anyone extending this:
a new facet must be reducible to a name, or it belongs in the payload store instead.

### D-254 — A region id comes from a scoped counter, never from the decision

> _2026-09-23 · core/semantic-log · active_

A region's `id` is minted from a counter installed fresh in each region scope (`withRegion`), not
from a global sequence and not from a position on the `Decision`: siblings number 1, 2 and a nested
branch is 1.1, so a position says where in *this* run's tree the record sat and nothing about
unrelated runs. `decision.seq` was the alternative and was rejected (D-251): it would have changed
R11's record shape and forced every consumer to interpret a number whose meaning depends on which
record is being read.

### D-256 — The receiver answers with its handler's progress

> _2026-09-23 · core/semantic-log · active_

A handler reached over the wire writes no records of its own, so what it announces through
`$meta.checkpoint` / `$meta.decide` used to be dropped with the ambient scope it staged into
(measured: 0 of 5056 retained records carried `progress`). Option 1 was chosen to fix it: the
**receiver** answers with that progress, in three parts.

`CallPhase` gains `answered` — the receiver's second record for the leg it was handed, beside the
`received` receipt it already wrote. The caller's `end` says the call came back; the receiver's
`answered` says what its handler did, which is knowledge only the callee has.

The adapter collects it *inside the scope the handler ran in* (`takeProgress`, once the handler
returns) and **re-stages** it (`attachProgress`) before writing the answer, so the answer carries it
as ordinary record progress. Re-staging rather than adding a second way of putting progress on a
record: the logger's own facet machinery does the rest, and a handler that announced nothing writes
no record at all.

The flow ledger keeps a leg's **progress cumulatively**. Its "one detail per call" rule (which
bounds what a chatty call costs) would otherwise drop the answer's progress, because the answer is a
later event on a leg whose receipt was already retained. Progress is a union by name — the same
point twice is one note — while everything else about a call is still kept once.

What this does **not** yet deliver: the *branch* a handler took. Points reach the answer and appear
as notes in the observed diagram (proven by `realm/blong-gateway/docs/observedMergeFlow.md`), while
the branch mark does not, so no `alt` block is drawn — see T-136.

### D-257 — A note is drawn over the participant that announced it

> _2026-09-23 · core/semantic-log · active_

A leg is recorded by both ends, so the note owner is carried on the model (INote {text, over})
instead of being read off the leg, which lands every note on the caller: the realm capture showed a
handler note over gateway while the handler ran behind the db adapter. Owner rule: a caller record
is its own from; a receiver record declares no target, so it takes the target the caller declared
for the same leg, falling back to the service that logged it. The collection is installed before the
handler runs (beginProgress) because enterWith cannot reach an already suspended frame. Considered
and not adopted: drawing a handler note as a leg to self, which the user had first imagined; the
note keeps the diagram readable and a leg-to-self rendering can be added later on the same owner
field.

### D-259 — A point is drawn with the record that claimed it, not where it was announced

> _2026-09-24 · core/semantic-log · active_

Points are consumed by the first record written after they are announced in a scope, so a point
announced before an outgoing call is drawn above that call, and one announced after it is drawn with
the answer of the call being handled. Live verification on commanderBranchList shows both halves at
once: three points announced before the dispatch ride the dispatch, and the point announced after it
rides the entry hop. This follows from takePoints clearing the holder, which is deliberate, and it
is the behaviour the ordering todo has to preserve while moving the milestones to the close of the
call.

### D-260 — A branch block shows every candidate, and labels the ones it never reached

> _2026-09-24 · core/semantic-log · active_

The mark carries every candidate the code declared, in that order, and the renderer labels an arm
whose predicate never ran, because evaluation stops at the branch taken: the chosen candidate
position is the whole of what is needed, so no extra field travels. This supersedes the first
reading of T-140, which truncated the list: the maintainer asked for the full candidate set with a
note on the arms that were never weighed, which is more informative and hides nothing, as long as
the drawing says what it means. Verified on the commander dispatch, whose block now reads alt
result-shape = array, else result-set, else empty — not weighed.

### D-261 — A branch block orders its arms so mermaid renders it

> _2026-09-24 · core/semantic-log · active_

Mermaid refuses a section with nothing in it when it is the last before end: the whole alt block
stops drawing. So the arms are ordered for the renderer rather than for the code — the empty ones
first and the one carrying the calls last, which is the arm that ran. Only the order changes: every
candidate keeps its label and the ones the decision never reached still say so, and a block whose
arms are all empty is given a note in its last one saying nothing observed yet, because a block
drawn around an exception has to show that it happened rather than fail to draw at all. Verified on
the framework flows (the hold arm now precedes hubB) and on the commander dispatch, and both the
artifact prose and the checkpoint concept doc say it.

### D-277 — Log cache retention deletes index files and reclaims old ones

> _2026-09-26 · core/semantic-log · active_

`core/semantic-log` retention now deletes an entry's index file when it prunes it, and a directory
that still holds the files of entries pruned the old way is repaired when it is opened.

The defect: `cacache.rm.entry` appends a deletion to the entry's index file and keeps the file. A
`cacache` key hashes into a file of its own, so a store keyed by unique ids grew one file per entry
ever written, whatever its bound did — 451 436 index files and 871 680 files in total for 10 001
live entries. Every `cacache.ls`, which is the pass at open that loads the retention order, read all
of them: 8.5 s before the first line a process printed, and about 36 s inside a tap run where
several opens overlap. `cacache.verify` does not repair it: it rebuilds the index from the entries
it can still read, so it walks entries and never the files that no longer hold one.

The repair reuses the measurement instead of a marker. The index scan is timed, and a scan past
`slowMs` is both reported at warn level and taken as the signal that the directory holds files left
by pruned entries; the dead files are then removed in the background, followed by `cacache.verify`
to collect the content they orphaned. A pass that removed something arms the next one, and a pass
that found nothing records that in `reclaim-state.json` and buys the directory six hours of quiet —
so a directory heals over as many opens as it takes and a clean one is not read twice. Pruning one
entry at a time is still what keeps the bound, and its removals are overlapped for the same reason
the reclaim reads with concurrency: a shared directory can hand one process a bound far larger than
its own writes left, and that step is the one an open waits for.

### D-279 — The store reads a secondary index, not cacache's own

> _2026-09-26 · core/semantic-log · active_

The store keeps a secondary index of the retention order in the cache directory (`order.jsonl`) and
reads that at open instead of `cacache`'s own index.

Why: `cacache` gives every key an index file of its own, in a directory of its own, so `cacache.ls`
reads one file per live entry — 10 251 files and 0.5 s warm for 10 001 entries, measured, and
2.3-2.9 s inside a tap child where the parent competes for the same disk. The walk is the cost, not
the reads: a sequential walk of the same tree took 620 ms on its own. The bound is what sets that
number (`limit` per surface), so the cost is linear in the bound, not in history.

The file is append-only: one line per write, one per removal. A small append to a file in append
mode lands whole, so two writers interleave lines rather than overwrite each other. This is exactly
what the store before `cacache` lacked — it rewrote its index per write, which is a single-writer
assumption, and it was retired for it.

The order is the position, and the line carries no varying field: `{"id","k"}` for a write and
`{"id","d"}` for a removal, never the time. An entry's place in the file is when it was written —
that is what last-line-wins means, and it is the whole reason a refresh is free — while the time is
already on stdout, and the cache's job is not to accumulate a second copy of what the console said.

A repeated write of an id is a refresh, not a second entry: it takes the newest place and the count
stays exact. The in-memory list needs to be told this explicitly — it is a list, and pushing a
second position for an id took the bound over by one and evicted an entry that should have stayed,
which a test now pins. The index gets it for free.

`cacache` stays the truth, and the pass that rewrites the file reads it first: being derived from
the truth is what makes a rewrite complete rather than one process's view of a store other processes
are writing to. That pass is due at open when the interval has elapsed (a day) or when the index has
grown past `ORDER_LINES_PER_ENTRY` times what it holds, and both triggers read the truth. Content
collection and the dated marker belong to the interval pass alone.

There is deliberately no pass inside a running process, which was the user's call between three
options. The reasoning is measured: the file grows only with activity — an idle development server
appended 0 lines in 50 s, while its startup burst had appended about eighty a second — so a
long-lived process accrues in proportion to what it logs and the next open bounds it with one
sequential read. A writer-driven pass would have to read the truth to be complete, which is the half
second the index exists to avoid, and it would make the writing process the compactor, which is the
single-writer assumption in miniature.

A directory without the index is read the expensive way once and given one: a directory written
before the index existed, or by a writer that keeps none. That read is the one reported when it is
slow, and the one that triggers the reclaim.

The cache itself holds one entry per emit and does not deduplicate similar lines: a record and a
payload are minted per emit (`mintRecordRef`, `mintPayloadRef`), and nothing keys the store by a
fingerprint. The "remove variable content so similar entries do not accumulate" goal is met in
*identity* — `serializeForIdentity` masks variable text — and so in the cluster service's registry,
which keeps one template per fingerprint and evicts by least-recently-seen with a monotonic recency
counter, so observing a shape again refreshes its template rather than creating a new one.

Measured on the real cache: realm start 1.21 s with no index, 0.67 s with one (the empty-cache
floor), and a tap child no longer reports a slow read at all.

### D-282 — The cache holds shapes: one entry per shape, plus a per-emit tenant

> _2026-09-26 · core/semantic-log · active_

The primary tenant is keyed by the shape reference (the 12-hex cut of the record fingerprint, which
is also refs.template), holds the newest occurrence of that shape and carries the number of times it
happened in its cacache metadata and in its order.jsonl line as n. A second tenant, bounded by its
own recordLimit, keeps a record under its own id when folding it into its shape would hide
something: it withheld a payload, or it carries an error; a record with no shape has nowhere else to
go and always lands there. The payload tenant is unchanged. The consequences accepted: stats() now
counts shapes (recordStats() counts per-emit entries), a record reference printed on a line resolves
only for the records that were kept per-emit, and the store is no longer the record of how often
something happened. That last one is what the flow tests had to change for: a cache that holds one
entry per shape cannot be replayed into the service to reproduce a burst, so the run ships to the
service as it happens (serviceUrl) and the burst is asserted from the occurrence count.

### D-283 — Bare semlog URIs; record link only when folding cost something

> _2026-09-26 · core/semantic-log · active_

The scheme is `semlog` and the kind is a one-letter path segment: `semlog://r/<id>` for a record,
`semlog://t/<shape>` for a shape, `semlog://x/<trace>` for a trace, `semlog://p/<id>` for a payload.
The `r=` and `t=` labels are gone because the URI already names the kind and the label stopped an
editor from recognising the link. The parent keeps its `p=` label precisely because it is not a URI
and resolves nothing. The record link is printed only when `denoiseHidesDetails()` is true, because
a per-emit entry exists only then, and an unresolvable link is worse than none. `src/refs.ts` holds
the segment map and `src/retention.ts` holds both questions (`shapeKeyOf` and
`denoiseHidesDetails`), which the store and the renderer both ask, so they cannot disagree about
whether a link resolves.

## Superseded

### D-281 — Shape-keyed retention in the log cache vs. occurrence counts

> _2026-09-26 · core/semantic-log · superseded_

Folding retention to one live entry per shape (implemented, version A: keys stay per-emit ids)
collapses occurrences as well as storage. Measured consequences: the flow test F2 'a retry burst is
one template at a rate-shift' fails because collected() reads the participant cache, so a 41-retry
burst ships one record and the R6b rate tracker sees one occurrence; logger.test 'a child shares the
family cache' fails because eight same-template debug lines retain one entry (size 1, dropped 0)
instead of five bounded and three pruned. The cache is the source from which records are shipped to
the detectors, so a cache that keeps one entry per shape cannot also be the record of how often a
shape occurred. Three ways out are on the table and the choice is the user's: (1) keep folding and
give each retained entry an occurrence count that the ingest and export paths read instead of
re-reading records; (2) fold only the content, keeping one record per occurrence with the key per
emit and one stored body per shape; (3) make the shape ref the key itself, which makes a printed
record ref stable and equal to the template ref.

Superseded by `D-282`.

The user chose option 1 and asked for the shape hash as the key, which is what D-282 implements: the
primary tenant is keyed by the shape and carries an occurrence count, and the per-emit reference
lives in a second tenant.
